# CR (Crane Company) — Value Investor Note

## Circle of Competence
Understandable at the business-model level: Crane Company sells niche, certified, mission-critical components across three segments - Aerospace & Electronics (sensors, actuators, power systems for commercial/military aircraft), Process Flow Technologies (valves and pumps for corrosive/hazardous chemical and pharma processes), and Engineered Materials (composite panels for RVs/trailers). No exotic financial engineering. The genuinely uncertain part is not what Crane does but whether the current growth and margin levels represent a new normal or a cyclical peak - that's the live question, not the business model itself.

## Moat & Durability — Score 7/10
Aerospace & Electronics is the strongest piece of the moat: once a part is FAA/OEM-qualified onto an airframe it cannot economically be resourced for the platform's 20-30 year life, and the aftermarket spares/repair tail that follows is high-margin and sticky. Process Flow Technologies has a real but narrower moat - engineers specifying valves for hazardous or corrosive service default to trusted, track-recorded brands because failure is a safety event, not an inconvenience, but competition from other engineered-valve makers is real. Engineered Materials (composite panels for RVs and trailers) is the commoditized, cyclical laggard of the three and drags the blended score down from where the aerospace business alone would sit.

## Management & Capital Allocation
ROE of 16.5% on moderate-to-somewhat-elevated leverage (debt/equity ~51%) is respectable but not spectacular. Operating margin of 35.5% and gross margin of 47% are strong for specialty industrials and, if durable, imply real pricing power - but margins this rich arriving alongside 25.6% revenue growth (unusually high for a mature industrial) is a combination that deserves scrutiny this single-snapshot packet cannot provide. No dividend, buyback, or insider-ownership detail is present, so 'trustworthy management' here is an inference from capital efficiency, not a verified fact from disclosed actions.

## Predictability
The packet is one dated snapshot (2026-08-15) with no trend history and a null thesis field. A 25.6% revenue growth rate could be a genuine aerospace build-rate/aftermarket inflection or a temporary comp/mix effect, and there is no way to tell which from this data alone - which fails Munger's 'easy decision' test on its face. Momentum data reinforce the caution: RSI 42.6 (neutral), momentum score 52/100 (middling), and roughly flat trailing-1-month performance despite a stronger 3-month run - the market is not currently paying up further for the growth print, which is itself informative.

## Inversion — How an Owner Loses Money From Here
1. **Cyclical peak mistaken for a new baseline**: the aerospace build-rate/aftermarket cycle rolls over (OEM production cuts, defense-budget timing, a fleet-grounding event) and the 25.6% growth print proves to be the top of a cycle, while the stock is priced at 28x forward earnings and 18x EV/EBITDA for durable growth, not a cyclical peak.
2. **Margin mean reversion**: a 35% operating margin is unusually rich for this business mix; if pricing power erodes or costs/mix normalize, earnings compress even with revenue holding up, hurting a stock priced on today's margin structure.
3. **Leverage amplifies a re-rating**: at ~51% debt/equity, a growth disappointment paired with multiple compression from a 38x trailing PE (a long way to fall) hits earnings and the multiple simultaneously.

## Valuation
The packet gives market cap ($12.62B), trailing P/E (38.17x), forward P/E (27.98x), EV/EBITDA (17.98x), and FCF yield (2.88%) but no share price or share count. Backing into per-share terms using an approximate ~58M diluted share count (a modeling assumption, not sourced from the packet, consistent with Crane Company's post-2023-spinoff share base) implies a current price near $218/share, trailing EPS near $5.70, forward EPS near $7.78, and FCF/share near $6.27. Haircutting FCF modestly for normalization gives owner earnings of roughly $6.00/share.

Two-stage owner-earnings model:
- **Low case** (5% growth for 5 years tapering to 3% terminal, 10% discount rate reflecting real cyclicality in aerospace/industrial end markets): ~$96/share.
- **High case** (10% growth for 5 years tapering to 4% terminal, 9% discount rate crediting the aerospace-certification moat and current momentum): ~$161/share.

Midpoint ~$128.5/share vs. an implied current price of ~$218/share gives a margin of safety of roughly -41%. A 2.88% FCF yield (thin relative to earnings-yield-implied multiples) confirms the market is pricing this as a growth compounder with a durable margin structure, not a value opportunity - and this packet cannot yet confirm either assumption.

## The Cloning Caveat
Dennis Hong of ShawSpring Partners opened a new position sized at 7.82% of the portfolio in Q2 2026 - a genuinely concentrated bet from a manager who runs a focused book, not a basket allocation. That is meaningful signal that a credible investor has done work (likely channel checks on the aerospace aftermarket cycle) we don't have access to here. But it is corroboration, not a substitute for price discipline: even a focused 7.82% bet from a respected manager doesn't change what the packet's own multiples show - a stock priced well above a conservative owner-earnings estimate, with growth and margin durability that remain unverified from this data alone.

## Verdict
**Pass, conviction 3/10.** A real, understandable business with a genuine moat concentrated in its aerospace segment, growing fast and printing rich margins - but priced at 38x trailing earnings and a 2.88% FCF yield that already assumes both the growth rate and the margin structure are permanent. Munger-strict discipline finds no margin of safety here (~-41% versus a conservative owner-earnings fair value range of $96-$161/share against an implied ~$218 price). Worth watching for a pullback or for a longer earnings history to confirm the growth is structural rather than cyclical, but not a buy at the current implied price.
momentum_thesis: CR's twelve-month tape is barbell-shaped: a 3-month sprint of +19.8% has done virtually all the work, implying the stock was roughly flat-to-down over the prior nine months of the return window, and that sprint has already gone quiet — the trailing month is up just 1.2%. Price sits 13.0% above the 200DMA, but RSI14 at 42.6 says the tape has cooled well before price has, a classic momentum-price divergence that flags stalling rather than continuation. Positioning offers no tailwind: short interest is negligible at 2.1% of float with only 2.1 days to cover, so there's no squeeze fuel, and a 4.69 put/call open-interest ratio is a meaningfully defensive skew for a name that just ran — options desks look to be buying protection into strength, not chasing it higher. ShawSpring's brand-new position sized at 7.82% of portfolio is a real conviction signal, but it reads as a fundamentals bet (25.6% revenue growth, 35.5% operating margin, 16.5% ROE against a rich 38x trailing / 28x forward multiple) layered onto a name whose price momentum has already stalled — a floor argument, not a momentum accelerant. Net: this looks like a name consolidating after a hot quarter, not one breaking out.
